methods.text: Read the brief aloud and mark every word that makes you hesitate.
Price each part before building it, and drop what costs more than it returns.
Describe the work to a colleague using only nouns and numbers.
Write the three questions a doubtful buyer will ask and answer each on the page.
Keep a log of every decision with its reason, and review it at the end.
Change one variable at a time and record the result.
Start with the dullest part and finish it completely.
Set every default value to the most common real case.

constraints.text: Readable at 200 percent browser zoom without sideways scrolling.
Every number rounds to at most two decimal places.

tasks.text: Churn cost calculator: customer count, monthly churn rate, and average monthly revenue per customer give the revenue lost per year and the gain from cutting churn by one point.
Price change simulator: current price, monthly volume, unit cost, and an expected volume change give revenue and margin at five price steps, side by side.
Error cost tally: errors per month, cost to fix each, and the share caught late give the monthly and yearly cost of mistakes, with each step of the sum shown.
Tool overlap finder: the buyer's current tools with monthly cost and main uses give the functions covered more than once and the spend that could be cut.
Rollout timeline builder: a start date, number of teams, and weeks per team give a dated rollout schedule with a buffer week the buyer sets, printable.
Single point check: the buyer's key tasks, who can do each, and whether a backup exists give a list of tasks that depend on one person, ranked by impact.

methods: Design the error and empty states first.
List the assumptions in the brief and check each one.
Make it work in black and white before adding color.
Take the conventions of a genre and break exactly one.
Write the copy before the layout.
Scope the work to what fits in one day.
constraints: Under 100 words of fixed text on the page.
tasks: Cost-of-inaction calculator: the buyer's current volumes and rates give what the problem costs per month and per year, with each step of the sum shown.
Readiness scorecard: twelve yes-or-no questions give a score out of 100, the three weakest areas, and one next step for each.
Benchmark checker: the buyer's own figures sit next to typical ranges they can edit, with each gap marked ahead, level, or behind.
Leak finder: a funnel of stages with counts gives the stage that loses the most and what fixing half of that loss would be worth.
Time-back calculator: weekly hours on manual tasks and an hourly cost give the hours and money an automated step would return.
Before-and-after map: today's process as a list of steps becomes a side-by-side view marking the steps that could be removed or automated.
